core: Globalization as the deepening integration of national economies through cross-border flows of goods, services, capital, people, technology, and information
Drivers: falling transport and communication costs, trade liberalization, global supply chains, and the internet
Benefits: faster growth, lower consumer prices, wider variety, and the large fall in global extreme poverty as developing economies integrated

Costs and criticisms: job dislocation and wage pressure in import-competing sectors of rich countries, rising within-country inequality, labor and environmental concerns, and exposure to global shocks
Positive record (growth, poverty, trade share) stated with dated attribution vs. the normative 'is globalization good or bad' verdict left contested

claims.claim: Globalization is the increasing integration of national economies through cross-border flows of goods, services, capital, people, technology, and information; a common summary measure is trade (exports plus imports) as a share of output.

Cross-border trade is historically recent at large scale: a long-run trade openness index never exceeded about 10% of world output before 1800, whereas today the sum of exports and imports across nations exceeds 50% of global output.

The United States is comparatively less trade-dependent than many economies: imports plus exports were about 11% of U.S. GDP in 1970 and about 32% more recently, while roughly 97% of Botswana's economic activity is connected to trade.

The global extreme-poverty rate fell dramatically over the long run and especially as developing economies integrated: from roughly 75% of the world's people in 1820 to about 10% by 2014, with reduction accelerating in the early 21st century.

By the World Bank's international poverty line the extreme-poverty rate fell from roughly 38% in 1990 to under 10% by 2019 at the $2.15-a-day line (2017 prices); the Bank revised the line to $3.00 a day (2021 prices) in 2025, under which about 831 million people were counted as extremely poor.

Integration also imposes concentrated costs in rich countries: rising Chinese import competition between 1990 and 2007 raised unemployment and lowered wages and labor-force participation in the U.S. local labor markets most exposed to it, and import competition accounts for about one-quarter of the contemporaneous decline in U.S. manufacturing employment, with local adjustment remarkably slow.

Whether globalization is on balance good or bad is a genuinely contested normative question; the empirical record (growth, lower prices, poverty decline, but also dislocation, inequality, and shock exposure) is cited by both defenders and critics, so no scholarly consensus resolves the value judgment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is globalization good or bad overall?
positions: Defenders emphasize faster growth, lower consumer prices, greater variety, and the historic fall in global extreme poverty as economies integrated.

Critics emphasize job dislocation and downward wage pressure in import-competing sectors of rich countries, rising within-country inequality, weaker labor and environmental standards, and vulnerability to global shocks.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a genuinely contested normative debate. The positive record is reported with dated attribution; the value verdict is named as contested rather than decided.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Poverty-line revision changes the headline poverty figure
positions: Older estimates used a $2.15/day line in 2017 prices (about 38% in 1990 to under 10% by 2019).
The World Bank raised the line to $3.00/day in 2021 prices in 2025, raising the counted headcount (about 831 million recently).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are reported with the line and price base named, so the long-run downward trend is clear without conflating incompatible thresholds.

sourceRecords.title: Extreme poverty: how far have we come, and how far do we still have to go?
sourceRecords.provider: Our World in Data (Max Roser), University of Oxford / Global Change Data Lab
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: about 75% of the global population lived in extreme poverty in 1820, falling to roughly 10% by 2014; it took 136 years (1820-1956) for the global rate to fall under 50%, then 45 more years to halve again by 2001; global poverty reduction accelerated in the early 21st century. Page notes it used an earlier World Bank release (2011 international dollars); the International Poverty Line has since been revised. Author Max Roser; CC BY 4.0. Figures described and attributed.

sourceRecords.title: Poverty: Overview
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports: the current international extreme-poverty line is $3.00 per day in 2021 PPP (revised in 2025 from the earlier $2.15/day 2017 PPP line); around 831 million people were counted as living in extreme poverty in the recent estimate; the page frames the 1990-2025 poverty trajectory. World Bank search result corroborates the earlier $2.15-line estimates: roughly 38% in 1990 to under 10% by 2019. Treated REFERENCE_ONLY; facts synthesized in original wording.

sourceRecords.title: The China Shock: Learning from Labor-Market Adjustment to Large Changes in Trade
sourceRecords.provider: David H. Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon H. Hanson; Annual Review of Economics, Vol. 8 (2016), pp. 205-240
sourceRecords.notes: Read via author-hosted PDF and abstract 2026-08-19. Supports: rising Chinese import competition between 1990 and 2007 raised unemployment and lowered wages and labor-force participation in the U.S. local labor markets most exposed to it; import competition explains about one-quarter of the contemporaneous aggregate decline in U.S. manufacturing employment; displaced workers did not quickly relocate, and local labor markets adjusted slowly, with depressed wages and participation for a decade or more. Copyrighted article; REFERENCE_ONLY, findings summarized only, no text reproduced.
